title: Redwood cost/economics discovery with Summit Capital
summary: Discovery call focused on per-token pricing, batching/caching levers, and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Customer has a constrained budget, wants predictable unit economics for high-volume RAG workflows. Agreed next steps: share pricing model spreadsheet, run small throughput benchmark, follow-up demo of Redwood Optimize recommendations.
next_steps: Jordan to send pricing worksheet and example cost model (by 2026-12-11)
Priya to schedule 1-hour benchmark run with Summit infra (target week of 12/15)
Summit to share current prompt set and traffic profile (Aisha)
action_items: Jordan: Send pricing worksheet and sample TCO model by 2026-12-11
Priya: Prep benchmark automation and small test harness by 2026-12-16

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Summit Head of ML), Ben Torres (Infra Lead), Carmen Li (Product), Evan Park (Finance)

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan with Redwood, AE, and with me is Priya and Liam on the technical side. How's everyone doing?
00:06 Aisha: Good thanks, quick intro — I'm Aisha, head of ML at Summit. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a RAG product, cost is like the biggest thing for us. Evan's here to ask the numbers.
00:14 Evan: Yep, budget constraints, need predictable per-unit costs for forecasting.
00:18 Jordan: Great, that's exactly what we wanted to talk about — how we think about per-token pricing and levers like batching and KV cache to bring down unit economics.
00:27 Priya: I'll do a quick framing on the workload assumptions — feel free to stop me.
00:31 Priya: From what you shared, it's heavy RAG: lots of doc lookups, medium prompt sizes, not huge completions but frequent calls, spikes during market open. That means tail latency matters and batching helps — but caching is actually where you get biggest wins for repeated prefixes and similar queries.
00:47 Ben: When you say caching, you mean the KV cache or a prefix cache? How persistent is that across sessions?
00:53 Priya: Good question — two things: prefix caching (we cache the input prompt embeddings or serialized prefixes) and KV cache for decoder state between tokens. For RAG, the prefix/cache hit rate on retrieved documents — if you see many repeated retrievals — can reduce tokens sent to the model. We typically model hit rates and show cost improvements as a multiplier.
01:10 Aisha: Do you have typical numbers? Like, if we have 30% cache hit rate, what does that translate to?
01:16 Priya: Ballpark — 30% prefix hit could reduce total token generation by ~20-30% depending on prompt structure. Combined with batching, you might see 30-45% cost reduction versus naive per-call pricing. But exact depends on prompt length, doc size, and your percentiles.
01:33 Evan: Ok but we need this in dollars. Our CFO wants per-10k-request cost at P95. We have an average of 2.2 requests/sec with spikes to 12 rps.
01:44 Jordan: Understood. Two approaches — Hosted will give you the simplest per-token pricing with built-in autoscaling; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and lower per-token inference cost but with fixed commit. Private is more for compliance and gives you control but adds ops and infra costs.
01:58 Evan: How big is the per-token delta? Like, hosted vs dedicated — are we talking 20% cheaper or 2x cheaper?
02:05 Jordan: Typical ranges we see: Dedicated can be 20-50% lower unit cost at scale compared to hosted, depending on commitment and model quantization. But you carry base costs (commit) and potential underutilization risk. Hosted is higher per-token but no commitment. Private can be similar to dedicated on raw inference cost but add network/ops and licensing.
02:24 Ben: If we do dedicated, what's the minimum commit? Our ops team hates long-term GPU leases.
02:29 Jordan: We have monthly and annual commit tiers. For Dedicated, teams often start with a 3-6 month trial size: it's more of a reserved GPU pool measured in vGPU/throughput units rather than raw GPUs. We'll model utilization — if you hit X percent utilization you get to the lower per-token. We'll send an example spreadsheet.
02:45 Aisha: Can you walk through a worked example? Our typical prompt + doc bundle is 480 tokens input, and generation is 180 tokens average. Retrieval adds ~200 tokens in context on average. So total envelope is like 860 tokens per call.
02:59 Priya: Great, that's detailed. So naive per-call tokens = ~860. If you have 2.2 rps avg -> that's ~68k tokens/minute? Wait, let me compute — 2.2 * 860 tokens * 60 = about 113,000 tokens/hour? Sorry, math off, 2.2 * 860 = 1892 tokens/sec, times 3600 = 6.8 million tokens/hour, hmm that seems high — ok let me re-evaluate.
03:22 Liam: quick calc: 2.2 requests/sec * 860 = 1892 tokens/sec; *3600 = 6.8M tokens/hr yes that's right, big numbers. If that's continuous, monthly burns add up quick.
03:31 Evan: That's why we're nervous. At Hosted list-per-token that could be a lot.
03:36 Jordan: Exactly. So this is where batching and caching are key. If you can cache retrieved doc embeddings and short-circuit some calls, and batch the remainder, you reduce the per-token bill. Also model choice (smaller quantized models) can cut cost per token.
03:49 Carmen: On model choice — do you let us route certain routes to cheaper models? Like low-value API calls to 7B quantized, high-value to the bigger models?
03:56 Priya: Yes — smart routing is in the platform. Per-route model pinning and automatic fallback. You can specify latency SLOs and cost targets and route accordingly.
04:05 Ben: What about quality tradeoff when using quantized models? We have strict accuracy needs for certain workflows.
04:10 Priya: We recommend running a split test — Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles based on your evals. For many RAG tasks, an 8-bit or 4-bit quantized 13B is often good enough; for critical workflows we keep the larger base model. We'll provide guidance and quality regression alerts.
04:26 Aisha: Back to numbers — can you give me a spreadsheet example? Our CFO wants a per-10k-req cost at P95.
04:33 Jordan: We'll send a workbook. Quick illustrative example: Hosted @ $0.00003 per input token and $0.00006 per output token (example numbers) — for 860 tokens that's ~ $0.03 per request. Dedicated might bring this to $0.02 per request at our recommended utilization with batching and caching giving another 30% reduction to $0.014. These are illustrative; we'll compute with your exact profile.
04:56 Evan: Those unit numbers are helpful. But what's the cost of cache misses versus hits? I want worst-case P95 pricing.
05:03 Priya: For worst-case, assume no cache hits and minimal batching — that is basically the naive per-token. P95 depends on your traffic burstiness. To control P95, we recommend a mix: Dedicated capacity to cover baseline, Hosted burst/backfill, and caching to flatten spikes.
05:19 Ben: So hybrid routing is possible — baseline on Dedicated, overflow to Hosted?
05:22 Jordan: Yup, that's a common pattern. It gives predictable monthly commit for baseline and avoids dropped requests during spike windows.
05:29 Aisha: On security, if we go Dedicated with overflow, is data crossing Redwood hosted? We have strict data residency and KMS controls.
05:35 Jordan: If you choose Dedicated in our cloud, data remains in your dedicated pool. For overflow to Hosted there is cross-traffic; we can mark overflow as no-logs or redacted. For strict residency, Private (VPC/on-prem) is the option — that keeps everything in your environment and integrates with your KMS/HSM and SSO.
05:51 Evan: How do you charge for Private? Is it a platform fee + infra?
05:54 Jordan: Private is typically an enterprise contract: platform licensing + support + ops fee; infra costs either customer-managed or co-managed. Often the per-token inference cost on Private is cheaper (you control hardware/quantization) but you add ops and infra amortization.
06:08 Ben: Any examples of customers doing Private purely for cost reasons?
06:12 Jordan: A few regulated customers moved to Private for compliance and ended up optimizing cost because they controlled utilization and hardware. But you need scale to justify the ops overhead.
06:21 Aisha: We don't have a giant infra org — ops overhead is a big concern. We're leaning to a Dedicated + Hosted hybrid.
06:27 Evan: From finance perspective, preferred predictable monthly commit but not huge multi-year lock.
06:32 Jordan: We can model a 6-12 month commit that steps up as utilization ramps — called a ramping commit. We'll show scenarios in the spreadsheet: utilization vs effective per-token cost and break-even points.
06:42 Carmen: Can you explain the batching impact? We saw in your docs that batching increases throughput but can add latency. Our latency SLO is P95 < 400ms end-to-end. Does batching break that?
06:51 Priya: Continuous batching in our runtime is latency-aware. Small micro-batches for short requests preserve latency; during windows of high concurrency batching is more efficient and still meets 95th percentile SLOs for many customers. For strict sub-200ms SLOs batching becomes limited; that's where Dedicated with reserved capacity helps because you get lower queueing overall.
07:11 Ben: And how do you account for tokens consumed by retrieval? In our RAG flow we do embed+search prior to model call — those embeddings also have costs if you use Redwood embeddings?
07:21 Jordan: Correct. Embeddings cost is separate per-embedding unit. Many customers run embeddings on cheaper models or compute offline; others use Redwood embeddings and we include them in the cost model. We can include the embedding ops in the spreadsheet.
07:32 Evan: For forecasting, we need a model of three scenarios: conservative (no caching, low batching), expected (30% caching, modest batching), optimistic (60% caching plus quantized routing). Can you provide those three scenarios?
07:43 Jordan: Yes — we'll produce those three with monthly TCO, expected per-10k-request cost, and break-even for Dedicated commit.
07:50 Aisha: Good. Also want to understand the QA/regression detection — if we quantize and route to cheaper models, how do we detect if quality drifts?
07:59 Priya: Redwood Optimize can run evals against your prompt sets and flag regressions; we can hook into your CI and produce alerts on metrics you choose. It helps you set quantization thresholds per route.
08:09 Carmen: Any talk of throttling? In high-spike events we need graceful degradation — not increased cost.
08:14 Jordan: We have built-in policies: rate limiting, queuing, automatic fallback to cached responses, degrade to cheaper model, or soft-fail with 503. You can configure per-route policies.
08:24 Ben: Back to bench runs — what's the approach to get us real numbers? We can give you an API key and test dataset?
08:29 Priya: Best is a small benchmark: you provide sample traffic (prompts and distribution), we run a 1-2 hour synthetic replay on Hosted and Dedicated sims to show throughput, latency, and cost. We'll quantify effective per-token costs under your traffic. We'll need a small infra collaboration for Dedicated tests.
08:43 Aisha: Sounds good. We can sandbox a week after we see the pricing spreadsheet.
08:47 Jordan: Perfect. Evan, any constraints from finance about examples you need?
08:52 Evan: Need per-10k-requests, monthly at P50 and P95, committed vs on-demand, and sensitivity to cache hit rate. Also want an amortized infra/ops number if we consider Private.
09:05 Jordan: We'll add those. Any other questions?
09:08 Aisha: Slight transcription note — sorry if names are off, I'm typing in chat — but big ask is to show the impact of a 40% cache hit and the overflow hybrid pattern.
09:17 Priya: We'll model a 40% hit and show baseline Dedicated + Hosted overflow.
09:22 Liam: Also we'll include a recommended initial Dedicated sizing to cover your baseline 95th percentile on normal days so you minimize overflow costs.
09:29 Carmen: One last technical: how do you measure tokenization differences across models? We saw token counts vary across tokenizers. That can change per-token billing numbers.
09:37 Priya: Good call — tokenization variance is included in the workbook; we run tokenization with the specific model's tokenizer when computing tokens. We'll surface effective tokens-per-request per model.
09:46 Ben: All right. Let's recap next steps.
09:49 Jordan: Recap: Jordan to send pricing worksheet and example scenarios by Friday (2026-12-11). Priya to schedule benchmark run for the week of 12/15. Aisha to send prompt samples and traffic distribution by Monday (12/13). Summit to review and we'll follow up with a 1-hour demo focused on Redwood Optimize outputs.
10:07 Evan: That works for us. Thanks everyone.
10:10 Jordan: Thanks all, talk soon.

Note: transcription includes occasional minor OCR-like errors and filler. There were short cross-talk bits around 03:20 where numbers were recalculated live.
